claims.text: Code Droid scored 19.27% on SWE-bench Full, according to Factory's June 18, 2024 technical report.
Code Droid scored 31.67% pass@1 on SWE-bench Lite, rising to 37.67% at pass@2 and 42.67% at pass@6.
In 39 SWE-bench cases (1.7%), Code Droid's patch exactly matched the oracle patch, and in 80 further cases it was similar to the oracle patch.
For the SWE-bench run, Code Droid received only the problem statement as a ticket, with no hints, test patches or oracle patches, and its internet access was revoked.

In 8% of SWE-bench tasks Code Droid failed to include the target file among the files it analyzed. In another 8% the target file was analyzed but not ranked in its top 5. In 6% of all cases the target file was a top priority but was not selected for editing.
Code Droid took on average 5 to 20 minutes to generate one patch, producing up to three patches per task before selecting the most promising one. The longest case took 136 minutes.
Token usage per patch averaged under 2 million tokens, with some runs consuming as many as 13 million tokens.

Code Droid scored 21.75% on a SWE-bench subset, compared with 18.9% for Aider GPT-4o and 13.86% for Devin. Factory cautions that the subset has a different problem distribution and should not be the sole performance indicator.
Code Droid can generate multiple trajectories for a task, validate them with existing and self-generated tests, and select the best solution.
Code Droid uses different LLMs from Anthropic and OpenAI for different sub-tasks and samples several models when creating candidate solutions, for diversity and robustness.

Factory's HyperCode system builds a multi-resolution representation of an engineering system, with explicit graph relationships and implicit latent-space similarity relationships, to give Droids codebase understanding. Its ByteRank retrieval algorithm uses this to fetch relevant information for a task.
Code Droid decomposes high-level problems into smaller subtasks and has access to developer tools such as version control, editing tools, debuggers, linters and static analyzers.

Most SWE-bench tasks are debugging-style tasks because of how the GitHub issues were scraped, whereas Code Droid is designed for migration, modernization, feature implementation and refactoring work as well.

Factory documents three deployment patterns: cloud-managed, hybrid, and fully airgapped. Droid runs on developer machines, CI, VMs and Kubernetes clusters, and LLM traffic can be routed through the customer's own gateways and providers.
In the fully airgapped pattern, Droid runs in an isolated network with no outbound internet connectivity.
Factory advises running Droid at higher autonomy levels only inside a sandboxed container or VM, never directly on a developer host or a machine with standing production credentials.

Factory-managed Droid Computers are persistent cloud environments that retain installed packages, files, services and configuration across sessions, and they auto-pause when idle and auto-resume when a session targets them.

Platform-managed Droid Computers use iptables rules to allow only the daemon port inbound and disable root login and password SSH. The factory-user account has passwordless sudo and could modify those rules.

Each Environment-backed Droid run starts on a fresh Computer created from the Environment's successful snapshot. Changes are not written back to the snapshot, and parallel agents do not share working-tree changes.

Droid's OS-level sandbox uses Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap with a seccomp filter on Linux and WSL2, and routes network traffic through an HTTP/SOCKS filtering proxy that allows only approved domains.
The sandbox's default policy allows all file reads, denies file writes except to the current working directory, and denies network access except to Factory and WorkOS authentication domains.

The sandbox has two modes. per-command (the default) confines each shell command and its children but leaves the main Droid process unisolated. whole-process isolates the entire Droid process and refuses to start if isolation is unavailable.
Subagents launched through the Task tool inherit the parent's sandbox policy, and hook commands are wrapped by the sandbox or blocked if it cannot be established.

Factory states that the sandbox is defense in depth, not a hard boundary around untrusted code. Allowed network domains can still leak data, and writes within permitted paths are not restricted in content.

droid exec is a one-shot headless mode for CI/CD and scripts. It is read-only by default, --auto low/medium/high enables edits with risk tiers, and --worktree runs jobs in isolated git worktrees. It stops and exits non-zero if an action exceeds the autonomy level, and exit code 0 does not mean the task succeeded, so results should be checked with tests or linters.
